def: Byte-addressable working memory inside an NVM subsystem, exposed as memory namespaces and accessed with the SLM I/O command set; used mainly by computational programs. Defined by the SLM Command Set Specification (Revision 1.3 in the 2026 set).

A namespace defined by the Subsystem Local Memory command set whose contents are addressed in bytes rather than logical blocks. Treated as working memory, not persistent storage; Linux exposes it only as a generic character device.
A Computational Programs construct listing ranges within one or more memory namespaces that a program may use for input, output and scratch data.
Optional memory in an NVMe controller that the host reaches by address through a PCIe BAR (located by the CMBLOC/CMBSZ registers), usable for queues or data buffers.
A region of host DRAM that the host lends to an NVMe controller (often a DRAM-less SSD) for the controller's own use, such as caching mapping tables; the controller accesses it by DMA.

The NVMe family specification (Revision 2.2 in the 2026 set) that defines management of NVMe subsystems out-of-band over MCTP (SMBus/I2C or PCIe VDM) and in-band via NVMe-MI Send/Receive admin commands.

DMTF protocol (DSP0236) that carries management messages between endpoints identified by Endpoint IDs, packetised with start/end-of-message flags, sequence numbers and tags; bound to SMBus/I2C, PCIe VDM and other buses.
A service processor on a server motherboard that monitors and manages the platform independently of the host CPU and operating system; the usual NVMe-MI management controller.
In NVMe-MI, an MCTP endpoint in the NVM subsystem, associated with a port, that receives NVMe-MI request messages and returns responses.
The CRC-32C value appended to an NVMe-MI message to protect it end-to-end, independent of per-hop checks such as SMBus PEC or PCIe LCRC.

A PCIe Message TLP whose meaning is defined by a vendor or standards body identified in its header; MCTP over PCIe uses Vendor Defined Type 1 messages with the DMTF vendor ID (confirm values in DSP0238).
A drive's identity and capability information (manufacturer, part and serial numbers, form factor) stored in IPMI FRU format, readable over the two-wire bus or with NVMe-MI VPD commands.
Firmware code supplied by a PCIe device through its Expansion ROM BAR (configuration offset 30h in a Type 0 header) that platform firmware can run, e.g. a legacy INT 13h handler or a UEFI driver.

An optional NVMe area, separate from namespaces, holding boot code that a simple host can read through the BPINFO/BPRSEL/BPMBL register mechanism without building admin queues; two partitions allow safe updates.

An ACPI table defined by the NVMe Boot Specification through which pre-OS firmware tells the operating system how it booted over NVMe-oF (host identity, interfaces, subsystems, namespaces, discovery), so the OS can reconnect.

A PCI-SIG protocol that lets a trusted execution environment establish trust in, lock, and run a device interface securely, together with SPDM and PCIe IDE. NVMe 2.4 adds a TDISP information package reporting controller state.

Public-key algorithms designed to resist attacks by quantum computers, such as NIST FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). The NVMe 2.4 release prepares asymmetric key exchange for PQC.
The post-quantum key-encapsulation mechanism standardised by NIST as FIPS 203 (August 2024).

As reported for NVMe 2.4: a virtual NVM subsystem (virtual SSD) exposed from within a physical SSD to a virtual machine, which can be migrated live to another SSD. Field-level definitions are in Base 2.4.

As reported for NVMe 2.4: a 'blueprint', identified by a 128-bit UUID, defining the features, identifiers and behaviours an Exported NVM Subsystem exposes; applied identically on source and destination during migration.

An NVMe Base Specification mechanism that prohibits selected commands or feature changes on selected interfaces; NVMe 2.4 reportedly adds persistence across reboots and virtualization-specific controls.
An NVMe feature in which the host supplies idle-time thresholds so the controller can enter lower (non-operational) power states on its own.
